`self.downsize` is redefined, overwriting the 4/5-argument version

Defining `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149 completely overwrites `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` on line 145. false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded when `I18n.translate` is called outside a controller request

`I18n.translate` only loads `config.locale` (`load_locale(config.locale) unless @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale)`), while fallback locales are only loaded via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` inside `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any translation performed in a background job (Sidekiq), rake task, mailer, console, or test that does not go through `ApplicationController#set_locale`—or that passes an explicit `locale:` option to `I18n.t`—will not have the fallback locales (such as `SiteSetting.default_locale` or `:en`) loaded into `@loaded_locales`. Because Discourse's `translate_accelerator` patch suppresses automatic `load_translations`, `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` will look up keys in unloaded fallback locales and return missing-translation results instead of falling back.

`Pluralization` is included before `Fallbacks`, breaking fallback when a locale has an incomplete pluralization table

In `config/initializers/i18n.rb`, `I18n::Backend::Pluralization` is included into `I18n::Backend::Simple` before `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks`. In Ruby's ancestor chain, `Fallbacks#translate` will call `super`, which invokes `Pluralization#pluralize` on the result. However, if a translation key exists as a hash in the primary locale with a missing plural form (or if `i18n.plural.rule` is missing for the primary locale and falls back to `:en`'s rule, which returns a key like `:one` or `:other` not present in the partial locale hash), `I18n::InvalidPluralizationData` is raised and is not caught by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` (which only rescues `I18n::MissingTranslationData`), causing a 500 error instead of falling back.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent zero-arg `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` fails to compile

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the method defined on the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` (line 160) has the signature `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`. This causes a compilation error (`method isConditionalPasskeysEnabled in class UsernamePasswordForm cannot be applied to given types; required: UserModel; found: no arguments`). Pass `context.getUser()` to match the superclass method signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` requires `user != null`, breaking passkey login on initial authentication

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. During a normal (non-re-authentication) login, `context.getUser()` is `null` when `UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate` and `UsernamePasswordForm.challenge` run, so `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` evaluates to `false` and `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never called. As a result, WebAuthn conditional UI attributes and the challenge are never added to the login form on initial login, completely breaking passkey authentication when no user is pre-selected. Additionally, when `user != null` (re-authentication), this check does not verify whether that user actually has a passkey credential (`webauthnAuth.configuredFor(...)`), so passkey UI will be rendered even for users without registered passkeys when realm passkeys are enabled. The condition should allow `user == null` or check `webauthnAuth.configuredFor(context.getSession(), context.getRealm(), user)` when `user != null`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets raise ValueError when slicing a Django QuerySet

Both `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (when `enable_advanced_features` is enabled and `cursor.offset < 0`, or when `cursor.is_prev` is True) and `BasePaginator.get_result` (line 182, when `cursor.is_prev` is True and `offset < 0`) pass a negative `start_offset` (and potentially a negative `stop`) directly to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly forbids negative slice bounds and raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, resulting in an unhandled 500 error whenever a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator fails with TypeError when ordering by a datetime field

`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` passes `order_by="-datetime"` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, where `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime.datetime` instance. Unlike `DateTimePaginator`, `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` passes `getattr(item, self.key)` directly to `math.floor` / `math.ceil`, which raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime` as soon as any audit log row is processed. In addition, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw numeric `cursor.value` instead of converting it back to a `datetime`, which causes `build_queryset` to compare a `datetime` column against an integer on subsequent pages. `OptimizedCursorPaginator` should either subclass `DateTimePaginator` or handle `datetime` values when converting to and from cursor keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shared cache key uses Python's randomized `hash()` and caches stale allowlist state across processes

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` build the shared-cache key with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. In Python 3, `hash()` is salted per process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`) and only affects tuples when they contain hashed elements or across interpreter restarts/hash-seed differences; more importantly, `hash()` can collide across different project-id tuples, causing an organization's query over an un-allowlisted project set to reuse a cached `True` from a different project set. Furthermore, `sentry.options.get(...)` already has an in-memory TTL cache backed by `default_store`, and nothing in the codebase calls `invalidate_upsampling_cache` when the option `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is updated, so this extra cache layer both risks cross-project collisions and serves stale results in tests and production (for example, in `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest`, if two tests in the same process used the same `(org.id, project_ids)` pair with different mocked option values, the second test would read the first test's cached result).

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling check uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset` and ignores the rewritten `query`

Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` is called with the outer `dataset` and `request` rather than the `scoped_dataset` and `query` passed into `_get_event_stats`. When `get_event_stats_factory` splits a dashboard widget query (lines 362-452), it calls `_get_event_stats` with `scoped_dataset=discover` and a modified `query` (e.g. `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` or `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"`), while the outer `dataset` is `metrics_enhanced_performance` or `metrics_performance`. Because `dataset` is not `errors` or `discover`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` always returns `False` for those split queries; conversely, if `request.GET["query"]` contained `event.type:error` and `_get_event_stats` was called for the transactions-only split query, checking `request` instead of `query` would wrongly treat the transaction query as an error query.

Accidental git submodule `sentry-repo` committed to the repository root

The commit adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink/subproject pointing to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. `upsampled_count` sums `sample_weight` without handling `0` or NULL/default weights for non-sampled events

`upsampled_count` is defined as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with `private=False` (the default on `SnQLFunction`). For events in allowlisted projects that were ingested before client error sampling was enabled or from SDKs that do not send a sample rate, `sample_weight` in Snuba can be `0` or unset, causing `sum(sample_weight)` to count those events as `0` instead of `1` (e.g. `sum(if(greater(sample_weight, 1), sample_weight, 1))` or `coalesce`). Additionally, omitting `private=True` exposes `upsampled_count()` as a user-queryable function on the discover dataset for any organization, bypassing the project allowlist check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`fetch_error_details` pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` instead of matching by node id

`nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by `node_id` whose keys and ordering are not guaranteed to align 1-to-1 with `error_ids` (for example, implementations that omit missing keys or return keys in arbitrary order). Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore associate an `event_id` with the wrong event payload or silently drop tail items. Look up each `node_id` in `events` (e.g. `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids): data = events.get(node_id)`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutual exclusion check between `age` and `timestamp` ignores `0`

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` use truthiness checks (`if self.initial_data.get("age"):` and `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp"):`) instead of checking for key presence or `is not None`. Because `0` is a valid integer value for both `age` (a report generated 0ms ago) and `timestamp` (`min_value=0`), a payload containing `{"age": 0, "timestamp": 1640995200000}` (or vice versa) will bypass the mutual-exclusion validation and be accepted with both fields present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

false_positives.candidate:
First E2E test does not close backup codes modal and uses an unawaited promise in expect

In `apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts` (lines 52-53), after `fillOtp` completes in the first test (`"should allow a user to enable 2FA and login using 2FA"`), the modal transitions to the new `DisplayBackupCodes` step, which keeps the modal open and blocks `onEnable()` from being called until the user clicks `[data-testid="backup-codes-close"]` (unlike the second test at line 125). The test only passes because `expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` checks the truthiness of an unawaited `Promise<boolean>` (which is always truthy) instead of `await expect(page.locator(...)).toBeChecked()`, and the subsequent step immediately navigates away with `page.goto("/auth/logout")`.

PasswordField type prop is overridden when props.type is passed

In `EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx` (line 176), `<PasswordField type="password" ... />` is rendered. In `PasswordField` (`packages/ui/components/form/inputs/Input.tsx`), `{...props}` is spread after `type={isPasswordVisible ? "text" : "password"}` on `<InputField>`. When `type="password"` is passed by the caller, it overwrites the computed `type` attribute, so clicking the show/hide password eye button in `EnableTwoFactorModal` has no effect and the password stays masked.

When a user with a third-party identity provider (e.g., Google or SAML) and 2FA enabled logs in, they are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>`, which sets `totpEmail`. In `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx` (lines 180-182), `ExternalTotpFooter` is rendered instead of `TwoFactorFooter` when `totpEmail` is set, so the "Lost access" button to enter a backup code is never shown. true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses `[z.string().toString()]` as object keys, evaluating to `"[object Object]"`

In `minimumTokenResponseSchema`, the computed property names `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate at runtime to the literal string key `"[object Object]"`. Because `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, parsing any token response with `minimumTokenResponseSchema` strips the actual expiry field (e.g. `expires_in` or `expiry_date`) and every other field except `access_token`. To allow arbitrary additional fields or numeric expiry fields, use `.passthrough()` or `.catchall(...)` instead of computed keys on `z.string()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Caller-appended SQL clauses can bypass authorization due to unparenthesized OR expressions

`getAuthorizationConditions`, `getFilterConditions`, and `getBaseConditions` (when `filterConditions` is `null`) return `Prisma.Sql` fragments that have top-level `OR` operators without outer parentheses—for example, `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` returns `(("teamId" = ANY($1)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (("userId" = ANY($2)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false))`, and `buildFilterConditions` with only `eventTypeId` returns `("eventTypeId" = $1) OR ("eventParentId" = $1)`. Because SQL `AND` has higher precedence than `OR`, any caller that interpolates `getBaseConditions()` into a query alongside additional `WHERE` predicates (e.g., `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" >= ${startDate}`) will only apply the trailing `AND` predicate to the right-hand branch of the `OR`, causing the left-hand branch to ignore the additional filter or authorization constraint. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working hours check in `checkIfIsAvailable` uses `slotStartTime` for `end` and rejects valid split schedules

In `checkIfIsAvailable` (lines 138-151):
1. Line 142 computes `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` instead of using `slotEndTime`, so it never verifies that the end of the slot fits within `workingHour.endTime`.

Because it uses `workingHours.find(...)` to look for a violated entry rather than checking whether *some* working-hour interval contains the slot (`!workingHours.some(...)`), any user with multiple working-hour blocks on the same day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) will have every slot rejected: a morning slot fails the afternoon block's `start < workingHour.startTime` check, and an afternoon slot fails the morning block's `end > workingHour.endTime` check.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs object reference comparison and boundary checks in date override validation are broken

Inside the `dateOverrides.find` callback in `checkIfIsAvailable`:
1. Line 114 compares two fresh Dayjs instances with `===` (`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which compares object references and is always `false`. An all-day 'unavailable' date override (where `start` and `end` are equal) is therefore never detected as Equal, and if a slot happens to match that timestamp it won't be rejected.
2. Lines 118-125 reject a slot only when `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` or `slotStartTime > overrideEnd` (i.e. completely disjoint from the override), rather than when `slotStartTime < overrideStart || slotEndTime > overrideEnd`. Slots that only partially overlap the date override window, or that start at `overrideEnd`, are treated as valid.
3. Using `.find()` means that if a user has multiple date override ranges on the same day, the first range that does not contain the slot causes `find` to return truthy and the whole check to return `false`, even if the slot falls inside a second override range on that day.

false_positives.candidate:
Kafka consumer commit is invoked from a background thread instead of Arroyo's main loop

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background thread (`self.commit_thread`) that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes Arroyo's `Commit` callback. In Arroyo, `KafkaConsumer` (wrapping `confluent_kafka.Consumer`) is not thread-safe and expects `commit` to be called on the main `StreamProcessor` thread (typically inside `poll()` or `submit()`). Calling `commit` from a separate thread races with `consumer.poll()` / rebalance callbacks in `StreamProcessor` and can also commit offsets after partition revocation.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory

`FixedQueuePool` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected` or blocks. Because `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka as fast as `submit()` returns, the consumer will read messages into memory at Kafka network speed regardless of how slowly `OrderedQueueWorker` threads process them (contrary to the docstring claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). Under load or a slow downstream dependency, this will buffer an unbounded number of messages in memory until the process OOMs, and during `close()`/`join()` the workers cannot drain before `join_timeout`.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining queues, dropping queued items

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on every worker before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, any worker that finishes its current item (or wakes up from `q.shutdown`) immediately exits the `while` loop without draining the remaining items in `work_queue`, and without calling `join()`'s final offset commit. Consequently, on graceful shutdown (`close()`/`join()`), all still-queued messages are abandoned and completed offsets after the last 1-second tick are never committed.

`FixedQueuePool` is instantiated on the factory and destroyed on the first partition rebalance

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` / `terminate()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. In Arroyo, `create_with_partitions` is called every time partitions are assigned, and `close()`/`terminate()` is called on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked or rebalanced. After the first rebalance, `self.queue_pool` has all of its queues and worker threads permanently shut down (and `offset_tracker` retains stale offsets from the old assignment), so subsequent strategies created by `create_with_partitions` will raise `queue.ShutDown` on `submit()` and stop processing any messages.

`OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` gets permanently stuck if a partition has non-contiguous offsets

`get_committable_offsets()` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` and breaks as soon as an integer is not in `all_offsets`. In Kafka, offsets within a partition are not guaranteed to be strictly consecutive integers (for example, compacted topics, transactional markers/control batches, or filtered messages that were not submitted). Furthermore, when a consumer starts up or rebalances and receives its first message at offset `N`, `last_committed` is `-1` and `min_offset` is `N`, which works for the first batch; however, if any single offset number is missing between two messages (or if a partition is reassigned at a higher offset after `last_committed` was set), `offset in all_offsets` is `False`, the loop breaks immediately, `highest_committable` never advances, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and no further offsets are ever committed for that partition.

false_positives.candidate:
Kafka consumer commit is invoked from a background thread instead of Arroyo's main loop

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background thread (`self.commit_thread`) that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes Arroyo's `Commit` callback. `FixedQueuePool` is instantiated on the factory and destroyed on the first partition rebalance

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` / `terminate()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. In Arroyo, `create_with_partitions` is called every time partitions are assigned, and `close()`/`terminate()` is called on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked or rebalanced. After the first rebalance, `self.queue_pool` has all of its queues and worker threads permanently shut down (and `offset_tracker` retains stale offsets from the old assignment), so subsequent strategies created by `create_with_partitions` will raise `queue.ShutDown` on `submit()` and stop processing any messages.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory

`FixedQueuePool` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected` or blocks. Because `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka as fast as `submit()` returns, the consumer will read messages into memory at Kafka network speed regardless of how slowly `OrderedQueueWorker` threads process them (contrary to the docstring claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). Under load or a slow downstream dependency, this will buffer an unbounded number of messages in memory until the process OOMs, and during `close()`/`join()` the workers cannot drain before `join_timeout`.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining queues, dropping queued items

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on every worker before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, any worker that finishes its current item (or wakes up from `q.shutdown`) immediately exits the `while` loop without draining the remaining items in `work_queue`, and without calling `join()`'s final offset commit. Consequently, on graceful shutdown (`close()`/`join()`), all still-queued messages are abandoned and completed offsets after the last 1-second tick are never committed.

`OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` gets permanently stuck if a partition has non-contiguous offsets

`get_committable_offsets()` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` and breaks as soon as an integer is not in `all_offsets`. In Kafka, offsets within a partition are not guaranteed to be strictly consecutive integers (for example, compacted topics, transactional markers/control batches, or filtered messages that were not submitted). Furthermore, when a consumer starts up or rebalances and receives its first message at offset `N`, `last_committed` is `-1` and `min_offset` is `N`, which works for the first batch; however, if any single offset number is missing between two messages (or if a partition is reassigned at a higher offset after `last_committed` was set), `offset in all_offsets` is `False`, the loop breaks immediately, `highest_committable` never advances, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and no further offsets are ever committed for that partition.

Kafka consumer commit is invoked from a background thread instead of Arroyo's main loop

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background thread (`self.commit_thread`) that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes Arroyo's `Commit` callback. In Arroyo, `KafkaConsumer` (wrapping `confluent_kafka.Consumer`) is not thread-safe and expects `commit` to be called on the main `StreamProcessor` thread (typically inside `poll()` or `submit()`). Calling `commit` from a separate thread races with `consumer.poll()` / rebalance callbacks in `StreamProcessor` and can also commit offsets after partition revocation.

`FixedQueuePool` is instantiated on the factory and destroyed on the first partition rebalance

`ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` / `terminate()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. In Arroyo, `create_with_partitions` is called every time partitions are assigned, and `close()`/`terminate()` is called on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked or rebalanced. After the first rebalance, `self.queue_pool` has all of its queues and worker threads permanently shut down (and `offset_tracker` retains stale offsets from the old assignment), so subsequent strategies created by `create_with_partitions` will raise `queue.ShutDown` on `submit()` and stop processing any messages.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory

`FixedQueuePool` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected` or blocks. Because `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka as fast as `submit()` returns, the consumer will read messages into memory at Kafka network speed regardless of how slowly `OrderedQueueWorker` threads process them (contrary to the docstring claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). Under load or a slow downstream dependency, this will buffer an unbounded number of messages in memory until the process OOMs, and during `close()`/`join()` the workers cannot drain before `join_timeout`.

Furthermore, when a consumer starts up or rebalances and receives its first message at offset `N`, `last_committed` is `-1` and `min_offset` is `N`, which works for the first batch; however, if any single offset number is missing between two messages (or if a partition is reassigned at a higher offset after `last_committed` was set), `offset in all_offsets` is `False`, the loop breaks immediately, `highest_committable` never advances, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and no further offsets are ever committed for that partition.
